description:
Kaq Ulew Rovers (KUR) 

Es un equipo guatemalteco de ingeniería, agronomía y desarrollo de software. Desarrollamos una plataforma web interactiva con un visor 3D de Marte que integra datos geoespaciales de terreno y suelo para apoyar la planificación de asentamientos humanos, la gestión de recursos energéticos y la evaluación de condiciones de supervivencia. Su diseño modular admite nuevos datos y criterios ajustables, y se publica como código abierto para uso educativo y científico.
summary:
Marsway is an interactive web-based platform for 3D topographic visualization and the simulation of guided expeditions on Mars.

The application integrates digital elevation models (DEMs) from NASA Mars Trek, orbital imagery from HiRISE, geological maps from the USGS, and data from NASA Worldview and the Perseverance rover to reconstruct three key regions in 3D: Jezero Crater, Amazonis Planitia, and Utopia Planitia. Using an A* pathfinding algorithm, users can plot routes between two points—choosing between safe or fast paths—and toggle various layers of interest, while evaluating distance, estimated travel time, and an adjustable terrain-risk scale ranging from 1 to 5.

This project addresses the challenge of planning safe movement across the Martian surface by transforming open-access scientific data into an intuitive tool. Its significance lies in optimizing decision-making for future robotic and human missions, mitigating topographic risks, and making space exploration more accessible to students and the general public.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO AND HOW DOES IT WORK?

MarsWay is an interactive web platform for navigation on Mars, 3D topographic visualization, and expedition simulation, designed for planning and executing safe traverses across the Martian surface. The system allows users to explore three regions of significant interest covering areas of 2, 100, and 2,500 km²:

• Jezero Crater

• Utopia Planitia

• Amazonis Planitia

The interface combines a 2D cartographic view, a collapsible 3D topographic view (with vertical terrain exaggeration controls and Day/Night lighting modes), and an immersive 360° Street View-style view at Points of Interest (POIs). At sites where 360° panoramic photographs captured by rovers on the Martian surface are available, users can explore the environment at ground level to visually inspect relief, rocks, and obstacles before or during a traverse.

The entire operation is managed from Mission Control, organized into 5 main tabs:

  1. Layers: Allows users to toggle, combine, and adjust orbital layers (MOLA, CTX, and HiRISE), as well as topographic, geological, climatological/thermal (TES/THEMIS), and subsurface ice layers, along with preconfigured operational profiles (Mobilization, Exploration, Agronomy, and Custom).
  2. Route: Simultaneously calculates and compares the fast route and the safe route between two points using the A* algorithm, displaying detailed metrics for the active route (distance, estimated time, and risk level). It incorporates a real-time hazard reporting tool that allows users to flag unforeseen threats during the expedition—specifying the hazard type, its radius of effect, and its severity on a scale of 1 to 5—to dynamically recalculate the trajectory avoiding the affected area.
  3. Mission: Configures simulated expeditions from point A to point B (with an option for a round trip) by selecting from three exploration modes: EVA (extravehicular activity for astronauts), LRV (crewed rover vehicle), or Robotic Rover. Each mode offers editable parameters that affect effective distance, travel time, and equipment wear, and includes the option to enable scientific research during the traverse.
  4. Vehicle: Provides real-time execution controls to start, pause, or stop the traverse, as well as adjust the simulation time scale for both the outbound and return legs.
  5. Data: Centralizes the management and inspection of points of interest (including access to 360° panoramic views), hazard zones, soil/agronomy, local weather (atmospheric dust opacity Tau), and JSON state import/export.

Divided into two sub-tabs:

• Control Center: Allows users to view and download the technical and scientific report generated at the end of missions that had scientific research enabled.

• Geochemistry and Resources: Allows users to inspect points on the 2D/3D map to consult scientific evidence and coverage limits (perchlorates and oxychlorides observed by PIXL/SHERLOC, regolith properties, mineral hydration, SWIM ice consistency, and THEMIS thermal inertia).

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT OFFER AND WHAT IS ITS EXPECTED IMPACT?

MarsWay transforms complex planetary data into an intuitive operational tool that bridges the orbital perspective with real ground-level vision. It enables users to evaluate trade-offs between speed, topographic safety, and mechanical wear before and during a traverse. Its impact spans two fronts: supporting decision-making, visual terrain reconnaissance, and real-time contingency management for future robotic and crewed missions, and democratizing access to Martian exploration for students, researchers, and the general public.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, AND DATA USED

The platform was developed as an interactive web application using standard web technologies (HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript) with in-browser cartographic visualization, 3D rendering, and 360° panoramic viewer engines, Digital Elevation Model processing (20 m CTX DEM from Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation / PDS), and a custom implementation of the A* pathfinding algorithm with slope weighting, equipment wear, and dynamic exclusion zones. It utilized WMTS services and open scientific datasets from NASA Mars Trek (MOLA, CTX, HiRISE), panoramic imagery and data from Mars 2020 Perseverance (PIXL, SHERLOC, and navigation cameras), TES/THEMIS climatology and mineralogy, SWIM ice maps, and geological mapping from USGS Astrogeology.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED BY THE TEAM

The creativity of MarsWay lies in integrating a 3D topographic twin, 360° Street View-style panoramic views with real rover photography, a live hazard avoidance engine, and a multi-mode simulator (EVA, LRV, and Rover) with automatic downloadable scientific report generation into a single environment. During its design, the team accounted for critical real-world factors of Martian exploration: the correlation between the orbital map and the actual ground-level view; the differences in autonomy and vulnerability among astronauts on foot, crewed vehicles, and rovers; progressive equipment wear; environmental conditions such as atmospheric dust (Tau) and day/night cycles; and the scientific rigor of distinguishing between localized in-situ measurements and regional orbital coverage.
